1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6.name: Dutch Defence: Normal Variation
1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and controls e4 and d5, which makes White's central break with e4 harder. The knight commits to no pawn structure, so every Dutch set-up stays open for Black, from a solid Stonewall to a fianchetto. In return Black must find a way to fight for the centre with the f-pawn already advanced.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop, which can now develop with check on b4, and supports a later ...d5 in a Stonewall set-up. The pawn hems in the c8-bishop, but Black gets a solid, flexible game and keeps both knights' best squares free.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop for the Leningrad set-up and keeps a second plan: the knight can go to h6, delaying castling and leaving the c- and d-pawns to fight for the centre. The cost is time, as White gets room to take central space.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 d6.strategy: Prepares ...e5 and keeps the knight's development for later, but commits the d-pawn before the knight is out. An immediate ...e5 allows dxe5 dxe5 Qxd8+ Kxd8, which takes away Black's right to castle.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5, backed by the c-pawn, for a solid wall of pawns across the centre. It is slow, though: the knight loses c6, Black's pieces are still undeveloped, and White develops freely.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, which joins the f-pawn in controlling e4 from the long diagonal, an idea borrowed from the Queen's Indian. It is slow and leaves the centre to White, who can blunt the bishop with d5.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 before any piece is out. White can take the pawn, and Black then spends time regaining it, or push on and close the centre, in a structure where Black's f-pawn has already moved.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nc6.strategy: Hits d4, but 3.d5 drives the knight away: after 3...Ne5, 4.Qd4 attacks it and guards c4, so Black loses time while White gains space in the centre.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 d5.strategy: Challenges the centre at once, but 3.cxd5 makes Black spend time regaining the pawn, and 3...Qxd5 is met by 4.Nc3 with tempo. Together with ...f5, the move leaves e5 and e6 without pawn cover.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 e5.strategy: Offers a pawn to break up the centre, but 3.dxe5 simply takes it and White can hold it with natural development. With ...f5 already played, Black's kingside is loosened for little.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where its only forward squares are b4 and c5, far from the e4 and d5 squares Black needs to contest. The tempo is better spent on a more central development.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nh6.strategy: Heads for f7 to support ...e5, but the knight is exposed on the rim: 3.Bxh6 gxh6 leaves Black with doubled, isolated h-pawns and a broken kingside.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 a6.strategy: A waiting move that controls b5 and may prepare ...b5 against c4, but it develops nothing while Black's development has barely begun and White already holds the pawn centre.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 a5.strategy: Gains a little queenside space and secures b4 for a knight on a6, but it is a tempo spent on the flank while the kingside pieces stay at home and White builds the centre.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 h6.strategy: Takes g5 from White's bishop, but this slow prophylaxis leaves the centre to White, who builds it up while Black's knights are still at home.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 h5.strategy: Takes g4 from White's pieces but develops nothing, and with the f-pawn already gone from f7 it leaves g5 and g6 without pawn cover for good.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Kf7.strategy: Gives up the right to castle for good and develops nothing. On f7 the king stands on the a2-g8 diagonal and can be checked by a knight from e5 or g5.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 b5.strategy: Offers a pawn for nothing concrete: after 3.cxb5 Black has no developed pieces to use the open lines, and White keeps the d4 centre and an extra pawn.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 g5.strategy: Loses a pawn at once: 3.Bxg5 wins it, since nothing protects g5 and Black cannot recapture. The kingside is also weakened for good.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 f4.strategy: Gains space but leaves the pawn undefended: 3.Bxf4 wins it along the open c1-h6 diagonal, and Black has no developed piece to offer compensation.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3.strategy: A natural developing move: the knight takes control of e4 and d5, and White stays free to fianchetto the bishop or to build a broad centre. Black has not yet developed the knight, so White can also play for space in the centre.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 g6 3.g3.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto: the bishop on g2 will rule the long diagonal and e4, the square the f-pawn fights for, and the king can castle early. The game is slow and positional, with White playing in the centre and on the queenside while Black aims for the e5 break and a kingside attack.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight, covering e5 and h4 and keeping both the fianchetto and a quicker e3 open. It creates no threat, but it leaves White flexible and takes away the e5 square from Black before the dark-squared bishop is out.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 g6 3.h4.strategy: Starts a pawn storm at once: the pawn heads for h5 to attack g6 and open the h-file before Black has castled. White leaves development for later and gains space and kingside pressure, and Black has to react accurately, since passive play lets the storm grow.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Nh6.name: Dutch Defence: Bladel Variation
1.d4 f5 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Nh6.background: Max Euwe introduced it against Salo Flohr in a small tournament at Bladel in the Netherlands in 1969, held in memory of Richard Reti, and the game was drawn. The line has been played hardly at all since and has little established theory.
1.d4 f5 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Nh6.strategy: An offbeat try that parks the knight on the rim to keep f6 clear for the bishop's diagonal. From h6 it no longer watches e4, so White plays e4 at once and takes a broad centre with tempo, and Black is left passive and worse.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight guards e4 and h5, covering the diagonal that the f-pawn advance has weakened, and brings Black closer to early castling. Black builds a fianchetto set-up and plays for the e5 break and a kingside attack.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7.strategy: Fianchettoes the bishop at once, so it presses on the long diagonal against the centre, and keeps the knight's square open. The cost is that White gets time to expand in the centre before a knight reaches f6 to restrain e4.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3.name: Dutch Defence: Fianchetto Variation
1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3.strategy: The standard set-up: White prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, aiming it down the long diagonal at the e4 square Black's f-pawn tries to control. It is a flexible, solid plan that keeps the king safe and lets White choose when to challenge the centre.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.Nc3.name: Dutch Defence: Queen's Knight Variation
1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight to its most active square, adding to the pressure on e4 and d5 so that a later e2-e4 strike has support. The bishop on f1 stays at home for now, so White keeps a choice between a fianchetto and a more direct central game.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight to guard d4 and cover e5, and commits White to nothing else yet. The bishop can still fianchetto and the other knight can still choose its square, so Black has to settle the pawn structure first.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6.strategy: Props up the f5 pawn, guards d5 and opens the diagonal for the king's bishop, preparing a solid set-up with castling to follow. The price is a closed game: the light-squared bishop stays shut in behind its own pawns until the d-pawn moves.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 g6.name: Dutch Defence: Leningrad Variation
1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop: it will guard the king and press on the long diagonal. The cost is a looser kingside, which Black accepts for active piece play.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 d6.strategy: A flexible but modest move: it takes e5 under pawn control and frees the c8-bishop to defend f5, while leaving open how Black arranges the kingside. It does little else, and White completes the fianchetto and castles at leisure.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 d6 4.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop lines up on the long diagonal towards b7 and e4, and White needs only a knight move to castle. It is the natural development, and Black has to find a plan against a safe and flexible White set-up.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 d6 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight, which guards d4 and covers e5, with the bishop to follow on g2. White reaches the main set-up by a different move order and loses nothing against the quiet ...d6.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 d6 4.Nc3.strategy: Brings the queen's knight to the square that adds to the pressure on e4 and d5 and prepares the e2-e4 break. The bishop and the other knight follow, and the set-up is the main one reached in a different order.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 d6 4.Bg2 c6.strategy: Closes the long diagonal at c6, so the g2-bishop no longer eyes b7, and takes d5 away from White's pieces. A compact, solid answer that prepares queenside space and a queen move to c7, at the cost of delaying Black's own development.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 d6 4.Bg2 g6.strategy: Heads for the fianchetto set-up: the bishop on g7 will guard the king and, once the f6 knight moves, press along the long diagonal against d4 and b2. With ...d6 already played, Black gets a sturdy structure that holds e4 and e5 and a king that castles behind the fianchetto.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 d6 4.Bg2 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop and prepares castling, giving the classical shape: pawns on d6, e6 and f5 keep a grip on e4 and e5. Black accepts a slightly passive set-up for a safe king and the option of a later ...e5.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 d6 4.Bg2 c6 5.Nc3.strategy: Brings the knight out to add to the pressure on e4, supporting the e2-e4 break that is White's main way to challenge Black's grip on that square. White's set-up is complete apart from the king's knight and castling.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 d6 4.Bg2 c6 5.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight to guard d4 and cover e5 so that White can castle. Which square the queen's knight takes, and whether White breaks with e2-e4, can wait until Black's plan with ...c6 and ...d6 is clear.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 d6 4.Bg2 c6 5.Nh3.strategy: Aims for f4 and d3, where the knight would control e5 beside the fianchettoed bishop. The rim square delays natural development, and an immediate ...e5 takes f4 away, so the plan is slow and easy to disturb.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 d6 4.Bg2 c6 5.Nc3.name: Dutch Defence: Hort-Antoshin System
1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 d6 4.Bg2 c6 5.Nc3.strategy: Prepares the central break ...e5: once the pawns are exchanged on e5, the queen on c7 guards the square along the opened diagonal, so Black can challenge the centre without leaving a pawn loose. It is a compact set-up for a long manoeuvring game.

Builds the classical chain of pawns on d6, e6 and f5 and opens the f8-bishop, so Black can castle soon. It is solid but passive: White strikes in the centre with e4, and the bishop on e7 has little to do while Black waits for counterplay.

Switches to the fianchetto set-up: the bishop on g7 will guard the king and watch the long diagonal, while the pawns on c6, d6 and f5 already restrain White's centre. Black accepts a slower fight for the centre in return for a solid king and a bishop with a future.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2.name: Dutch Defence: Classical Variation
1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop bears down the long diagonal against e4 and the queenside, and White needs only a knight move to castle. White waits to see which pawn structure Black builds behind the f5 and e6 pawns.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight to guard d4 and cover e5, reaching the main set-up by a different move order. The bishop goes to g2 next, and White gives Black no new target in the meantime.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Nc3.strategy: Puts the knight on its active square, adding to the pressure on e4 and d5, but it invites ...Bb4, which pins the knight against the king. White must then spend a move to unpin, and ...Bxc3 would leave doubled pawns after bxc3.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Be7.name: Dutch Defence: Classical Variation
1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Be7.strategy: The most solid development: the bishop covers the kingside and prepares castling without committing the d-pawn. Black keeps the choice between a pawn wall and a more elastic set-up, at the cost of a rather passive bishop.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 d5.strategy: Claims the centre at once, fixing pawns on f5, e6 and d5 so that Black controls e4 completely. It challenges the c4 pawn immediately; the price is a shut-in light-squared bishop and a permanent hole on e5 that a White knight can use.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Bb4+.name: Dutch Defence: Nimzo-Dutch Variation
1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Bb4+.strategy: Develops the bishop with check before castling, so that White's queen's knight cannot come to c3 without being pinned. Black can later trade the bishop to double White's pawns or keep it aimed at the centre, at the price of time if it must retreat.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Bb4+ 5.Bd.strategy: The natural answer to the check: a developing block that keeps White's pawns intact, where Nc3 would allow ...Bxc3+ and doubled pawns. White accepts that the bishops may be traded, which eases the game for both sides.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Bb4+ 5.Nc.strategy: Blocks with the knight, which stays on the square that fights for e4 and d5. Black can take it: ...Bxc3+ bxc3 gives White the bishop pair and an open b-file, but the doubled c-pawns are a lasting weakness.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Bb4+ 5.Nd.strategy: Interposes the queen's knight, which then stands pinned against the king and shuts in the c1-bishop. Black can pile up on it at once with ...Ne4, so White has to untangle the pieces before developing normally.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Bb4+ 5.Bd.name: Dutch Defence: Nimzo-Dutch Variation, Alekhine Variation
1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Bb4+ 5.Bd.strategy: Retreats instead of trading, so White's Bd2 has cost nothing: Black has spent two bishop moves to reach e7 while White developed a piece in between. A safe way to reach the classical set-up, but it concedes a tempo.

Trades the dark-squared bishops at once instead of retreating, so Black loses no tempo and takes away the white bishop that would guard the dark squares. White recaptures with the queen or the b1-knight, and Black reaches a comfortable game with an easy plan.
Defends the bishop with the queen, so that 6.Bxb4 Qxb4+ trades the bishops with check. Black brings the queen out early instead of castling and leaves White to choose when the trade happens.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Be7 5.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight to its natural square: it protects d4, covers e5 and clears the way for castling. White gets a calm, harmonious set-up and waits for Black to commit the pawns.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Be7 5.Nh3.name: Dutch Defence: Classical Variation, Blackburne Attack
1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Be7 5.Nh3.strategy: Heads for d3 by way of f4, where the knight would control e5 while leaving the f-pawn free to advance. The rim square is awkward and the move delays natural development, which is why it is the less common choice.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Be7 5.Nc3.strategy: Puts the queen's knight on its most active square, adding to the pressure on e4 and d5 and supporting a later e2-e4. The king's knight and castling follow, and White keeps both a quiet and a direct plan open while Black's pawn structure is still undecided.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Be7 5.Nf3.name: Dutch Defence: Classical Variation
1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Be7 5.Nf3.strategy: Completes kingside development and moves the king off the e8-h5 diagonal that the f-pawn's advance has weakened. Black keeps the choice of pawn structure for the next move.

Builds the wall of pawns on d5, e6 and f5 at once, clamping e4 and blunting the g2-bishop's diagonal. The price is the c8-bishop shut inside the chain and weak dark squares around e5, which White's knight can aim for.

Controls e5 and opens the c8-bishop, and keeps the choice between a central break and a closed set-up for later. Black gives up the immediate clamp on e4 that ...d5 offers; in return the structure stays more flexible and no bishop is buried behind the pawns.
White castles too, tucking the king behind the fianchettoed bishop. Both kings are safe, and the fight is now over how Black arranges the d-pawn, which decides the character of the middlegame.

Develops the second knight to the square that fights for e4 and d5 and keeps castling in hand. Whichever pawn set-up Black picks, the knight already stands where it wants to be, so White reaches the main structures in a different order.

Supports the c4 pawn and prepares Bb2 on the long diagonal or Ba3 to challenge Black's bishop on e7. The plan is slower than castling and leaves the king in the centre a move longer, but it creates a clear queenside target.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Be7 5.Nf3.name: Dutch Defence: Stonewall Variation
1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Be7 5.Nf3.background: The traditional form of the Stonewall, with the bishop on e7. The Modern Stonewall, with ...d5 played earlier and the bishop on d6, was helped along by grandmasters such as Yusupov, Dolmatov, Short and Agdestein in the 1980s and 1990s and has remained more popular.
1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Be7 5.Nf3.strategy: Builds the pawn wall on f5, e6 and d5, giving Black firm control of e4 for a knight and a base for a kingside attack. The light-squared bishop is shut in behind the chain, and e5 becomes a lasting hole for White's knight.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Be7 5.Nf3.name: Dutch Defence: Alekhine Variation
1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Be7 5.Nf3.strategy: Occupies e4 at once, before committing the d-pawn. The f-pawn supports the knight, so White must challenge it or accept Black's grip on e4; Black still has to follow up with a plan for the centre.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Be7 5.Nf3.name: Dutch Defence: Classical Variation
1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Be7 5.Nf3.background: Black's 6...d6 is called the Ilyin–Zhenevsky Variation; it is less popular today.
1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Be7 5.Nf3.strategy: The more elastic alternative: the pawn takes e5 under control and frees the c8-bishop, keeping the e5 break available. It leaves e4 less firmly held than the pawn wall does, so White keeps chances to fight for that square.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 d5 5.Nf3.name: Dutch Defence: Classical Variation
1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 d5 5.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight to guard d4 while leaving c4 attacked for the moment: if Black takes it, White can regain the pawn with the queen. White heads for a slow, manoeuvring game against the pawn wall.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 d5 5.Nc3.strategy: Develops the queen's knight against the pawn wall, adding to the fight for e4 and d5 and preparing e2-e4 as a lever. White keeps the tension on c4 and the choice of how to complete development.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 d5 5.cxd5.strategy: Resolves the centre at once. After ...exd5 White has a half-open c-file to play on, but gives up the pressure that c4 puts on d5 and leaves Black a firm grip on e4 and a half-open e-file, which is why it is the less ambitious choice.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2.strategy: Puts the bishop on the long diagonal, where it shields White's king against Black's kingside play and, unlike a bishop on d3, is not blocked by the f5 pawn. The standard development against the fianchetto.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 g6 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight first, guarding d4 and covering e5, and keeps the bishop move for later. White reaches the main Leningrad set-up with the pieces in a different order.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 g6 4.Nc3.strategy: Brings the queen's knight to the e4 and d5 fight early, so that the bishop on g2 and the knight work together against Black's centre. A well-known order against the fianchetto, with castling and the king's knight to follow.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop guards the king and, once the knight leaves f6, bears down the long diagonal against d4 and b2. Black's play revolves around this bishop and a pawn break in the centre.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 d6.strategy: Controls e5 and opens the c8-bishop before the king's bishop goes to g7, reaching the fianchetto set-up by a different order. The central plans stay open, and Black castles into a compact position.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 c6.strategy: Blunts the g2-bishop's line towards b7 and prepares ...d5 or a queen move to b6 against d4 and b2. It commits the c-pawn early and delays the king's bishop, so Black falls behind in development against the quiet White set-up.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.Nf3.name: Dutch Defence: Leningrad Variation
1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight, protecting d4 and covering e5, and prepares castling. White gets a calm, harmonious set-up and waits for Black to commit the pawns.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.Nc3.strategy: Puts the queen's knight on c3 before the king's knight, adding to the pressure on e4 and d5 and keeping a later e2-e4 in reserve. White reaches the Leningrad main line by a different order.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.Nh3.strategy: Aims for f4, where the knight would eye d5, e6 and h5 while leaving the f-pawn free. The rim square delays natural development, and ...g5 or ...e5 can take f4 away, so it is less common.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.Nc3 d6.strategy: A solid, flexible reply: the pawn takes e5 and c5 under control and frees the c8-bishop to defend f5. Black keeps the kingside set-up open for later, and meets White's pressure on e4 calmly.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e6.strategy: Frees the f8-bishop with an eye on b4, where it would pin the c3-knight against the king, and keeps open a solid wall of pawns on c6, d5, e6 and f5. Black keeps a flexible, safe game at the cost of shutting in the c8-bishop.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6.strategy: Chooses the fianchetto set-up: the king's bishop will guard the king and bear on the long diagonal, and the f6 knight and f5 pawn hold e4 from the start. Black heads for active play on the diagonal and in the centre with a well-protected king.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.Nc3 d6 4.Nf3.strategy: The natural development: the knight protects d4 and covers e5, and White keeps the choice of fianchetto or direct central play open. White waits to see how Black deploys.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.Nc3 d6 4.g3.strategy: Switches to the fianchetto with the knight already on c3, so the bishop on g2 adds to the pressure on e4 and the long diagonal. The set-up is solid and flexible, and White still chooses between quiet manoeuvring and the e2-e4 break.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.Nc3 d6 4.Bg5.strategy: Attacks the f6 knight to provoke a concession: Bxf6 exf6 doubles Black's f-pawns but gives up the bishop pair. Black can drive the bishop back at once, and White has no clear follow-up, so it is sound but second-rate.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.Nc3 d6 4.Nf3 Nc6.name: Dutch Defence: Krause Variation
1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.Nc3 d6 4.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the queen's knight where it presses on d4 and prepares ...e5, challenging the centre directly. But the knight blocks the c-pawn and can be driven back by White's d-pawn, which gains space with tempo.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.Nc3 d6 4.Nf3 g6.strategy: Heads for the fianchetto: the bishop on g7 will guard the king and press along the long diagonal, and ...d6 already controls e5. Black gets the sturdy set-up the main lines are built on, with a safe king and a bishop with a future.

1.d4 f5 2.c4 Nf6 3.Nc3 d6 4.Nf3 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop and prepares quick castling, with the pawns on d6, e6 and f5 holding e5 and e4. A solid, classical set-up, at the price of a passive bishop on e7 and a slower fight for the centre.
